subject: research/impact-twin
professional: a contact-dynamics / nonsmooth-mechanics researcher (Acary-Brogliato or Stewart school) who has built time-stepping and event-driven simulators, plus a simulation engineer at a robotics group who tunes restitution in MuJoCo or PyBullet. They would check first that the closed-form truth is right, that the integrator comparison includes a properly second-order event-located scheme, and whether the O(dt) restitution and settling bias is new relative to the time-stepping convergence literature.

evidence.correctness: Ran the shipped code and recomputed independently with a from-scratch script (scratchpad ind.py, not importing the author's module). (1) Zeno time by brute-force summation of 20000 flights vs closed form: e=0.5 1.35457, e=0.9 8.57895, e=0.99 89.8532, all equal the README/results.txt values (1.3546, 8.5789, 89.8532). (2) d ln T/de by central finite difference of the summed series: 10.5263 at 0.9 and 100.5025 at 0.99 vs 2/(1-e^2) = 10.526 and 100.50 (README 10.5, 100). (3) My own clamp semi-implicit Euler twin and my own enumeration of exact flights: exact last time above 1 cm at e=0.9 = 7.66030 s (results 7.6603); twin error -0.19585 at dt=1e-2 (README -19.6%) and -0.01740 at dt=1e-3 (results -0.0174); apparent restitution at dt=1e-2 = 0.885889 (README 0.886, results 0.88589). Full experiments/run.py re-run in 0.2 s and its output is byte-identical to the committed results.txt (diff empty), so the headline numbers are deterministic and reproduce. Caveat, which is why this is not a 4: the exact comparison is a closed form the author derived, no third-party simulator (MuJoCo, PyBullet, Simulink Zeno detection) was used to check the twin side, and result 4 compares unlike quantities (see claims).
evidence.completeness: Claims checked end to end: closed-form truth (zeno_time, impact_time, last_time_above): works, consistent with brute force; three twin schemes clamp/mirror/locate: all run and produce the reported tables; step sweep 1e-2..1e-4 with five steps, three e values: present in results.txt; log-log slopes 1.11/1.12/1.00: reproduced by rerun; calibration experiment (bisection of e): present; impact-count and impact-time-error tables: present; README quoted commands: 'PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests' gave 'Ran 10 tests ... OK' in 0.004 s (README says 10, under 1 s: true); experiments/run.py 'a few seconds': actually 0.2 s. Whitepaper, SVG and figure.py exist; no TODO or stub. Not done and said so: result 7 mechanism ('not derived'), compliant contact, velocity-dependent restitution, multi-contact Zeno, any real hardware or engine data. The project is small (89-line model) but finished as scoped. Not checked: figure.py output beyond existence.
evidence.verification: 10 unittest tests, run: all pass. Seeded mutations, each reverted with git checkout (git status clean for the subject afterwards): (a) clamp restitution factor ×1.02 (-e*v2*1.02): FAILED, 3 failures. (b) settle_error_factor 2/(1-e^2) -> 2/(1-e): FAILED, 1 failure. (c) zeno_time ×1.001: not a clean failure; it makes the test helper exact_height spin forever (non-terminating loop between true and mutated Zeno time), so the suite hangs past 60 s: detected only by hang, a sign the test helper has no loop guard. (d) apex window changed from 'impacts == 1' to 'impacts == 2': FAILED, 1 failure. (e) mirror restitution ×0.97: 10/10 OK, NOT caught. (f) locate: contact fraction f = y/(y-yn) halved: 10/10 OK, NOT caught. (g) locate: impact velocity vi = v2 instead of the interpolated value: 10/10 OK, NOT caught. (h) no-op-ish penetration threshold -1e-9: OK (equivalent mutant, expected). So the entire 'locate' scheme, which carries headline numbers 2, 3 and 5 (-30.8% and the worst-variant claim), is not exercised by any test, and the mirror twin is only checked for sign of error at one coarse step (test requires only mirror settles later than exact). The paper's tables (apparent e values, errors at each dt, slopes, calibration, counts) are guarded only by results.txt being regenerated by hand, not by any assertion; no test asserts a single results.txt number. Score 2: the analytic truth and the clamp twin are guarded, the two other schemes and nearly every reported twin number are not.
evidence.craft: Read src/impact_twin/model.py (89 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, paper/whitepaper.md, pyproject.toml. Clean, dependency-free, readable, docstring states the model, deterministic, no randomness. Defects: no input validation (e outside (0,1), e>=1 makes last_time_above loop forever, e=1 divides by zero in zeno_time; delta >= h0 gives math domain error); simulate stores the whole height list (memory O(T/dt), fine here); run.py section 6 re-implements the clamp loop inline instead of calling simulate (copied engine, and it differs: it starts the first impact from v=0 identically but counts up to the Zeno time with no scheme option), so section 6 would not follow a bug fix in simulate; settle_twin silently returns 0.0 from last_above when the height never exceeds delta and returns the last grid index otherwise, with T=1.4*exact+1 chosen by hand and not checked to be long enough (if the twin is still above delta at T the 'settling time' is silently truncated); test helper exact_height has no loop guard (hang found by mutation c); the apex is read off the step grid, which the paper concedes makes e_eff non-monotone in dt. No unused imports found. Not a blocker, but a reviewer would ask for validation and for section 6 to reuse simulate.
evidence.claims: Checked README/paper claims against results.txt and my reruns: (1) rest-time sensitivity 2/(1-e^2): true, independently differentiated. (2) apparent e values 0.886/0.895/0.879: true. (3) settling errors -19.6/+4.0/-30.8 and -34.8/+46.3/-47.1, slopes 1.0-1.1, 0.1-0.3% at 1e-4: true as reported. (4) 'The restitution bias explains most of the clamp error (predicted -14.9%, measured -19.6%)': NOT a like-for-like comparison. -0.1485 is d ln T from the linearised Zeno-time formula, applied to the Zeno time T; -0.1959 is a relative error (twin-exact)/exact of the time to last exceed 1 cm, a different quantity (t_last at e=0.9 is 7.66 s, Zeno 8.58 s, and the 1 cm time has different sensitivity). In like units the measured value is ln(1-0.1959) = -0.218 vs -0.1485 predicted, i.e. the bias explains about 68% of the log-error, and the 'sensitivity' used is for the wrong observable. results.txt line 4(b) prints the two side by side under one label ('predicted linear change in Zeno time ... measured change in settling time'). 'Most' is a loose reading of a mismatched ratio. (5) 'does nothing at 1e-3 to 3e-3': true for clamp only (the sentence in the README abstract is unqualified; locate improves at every step and mirror changes sign); the paper text is accurate, the README summary compresses it misleadingly. (6) counts 238/444/688 and 43/65/87: true. (7) up to tens of steps: true (27.2). The 'first-order in dt' claim rests on a five-point fit of |error| including non-monotone cells (e=0.95 mirror changes sign and is not first-order monotone); the paper does flag the slope as measured on five steps not proved. Disclaimer present ('Stylised', affiliation disclaimer, no endorsement); upstream references real (Brogliato 2016, Goebel-Sanfelice-Teel 2012, Zhang et al. 2001, Stewart 2000). 'Builds on' names ARPG/HIRO/RECUV groups with the honest note that no paper from them is reproduced. Score 2 because headline result 4 and the abstract form of result 5 do not say what the numbers show.
evidence.fitness: A researcher building on this gets a tidy worked example showing that a naive fixed-step twin of a Zeno system is O(dt) biased in restitution and settling time, and that rest time is hypersensitive to e. Walked the job: I reproduced each table in 0.2 s and could extend to a new e or dt. But a researcher cannot take it to a venue or build a method on it: nothing is measured against a real engine, a real ball or a public dataset; the 'twin' is the author's own 30-line integrator. Nearest prior work: convergence of Moreau time-stepping and Newton impact (Paoli-Schatzman 2002; Stewart 1998, 2000; Acary-Brogliato 'Numerical Methods for Nonsmooth Dynamical Systems', 2008, which treats the bouncing ball with restitution and shows O(dt) order and Zeno handling), event-driven location and Zeno detection in hybrid-system simulators (Lamperski-Ames, Zhang et al. 2001 cited, Simulink/Modelica zero-crossing, Mirtich 1996 on impact), and restitution calibration in sim-to-real work (Hwangbo 2018 and the contact-parameter identification literature). The closed-form T=(v1/g)(1+e)/(1-e) and its derivative are textbook; the first-order bias is the known order of explicit time-stepping. What is new is only the finite table of the three crude schemes and the calibration counterexample at dt=1e-2; useful as a classroom warning, not a result. Score 2.
evidence.domain: A contact-dynamics expert would accept the model of Newton restitution and the closed-form truth, and the honest framing that locate is 'a crude implementation'. They would object: (1) the 'locate' variant uses linear interpolation of a quadratic trajectory, so it is a strawman; the standard event-located scheme solves the quadratic for the impact instant (exact for ballistic flight) and would be near machine accuracy until the Zeno region, which would reverse the 'locate is worst' ranking and the paper's implied advice; (2) real engines (MuJoCo, PyBullet, Drake) use compliant or complementarity contact with a restitution that is itself step-dependent (MuJoCo solref/solimp), not a post-step penetration test with Newton e, so the 'twin' studied is not a twin a roboticist runs (the paper lists this under next steps); (3) the settling threshold 1 cm and the clamp/mirror conventions are the author's choices with one drop height and one g; (4) result 5's mirror +53% is a bisection landing on a jump of a piecewise-constant apparent e (the paper says so), which makes it an artefact of the calibration procedure rather than a property of mirror twins; (5) the apparent-restitution estimator reads a grid maximum, so e_eff carries a dt-sized error of its own, comparable to the bias being measured at the finest steps (clamp e_eff at 3e-3 is 0.89962 and at 1e-4 0.89984, non-monotone). Score 2: the method is honest and sound for what it computes but would not be signed off as a study of fixed-step digital twins of impact.

defects.what: Result 4 ('restitution bias explains most of the clamp error: predicted -14.9%, measured -19.6%') compares a linearised change in ln of the Zeno time with a relative error of the time to last exceed 1 cm: different observables and different units (ln vs relative). Like-for-like in logs it is -0.1485 vs -0.218 (about 68%); the sensitivity 2/(1-e^2) belongs to T, not to t_last.

The entire 'locate' scheme and the mirror restitution factor are untested: seeded mutations (halved contact fraction, impact velocity replaced by v2, mirror e x0.97) left 10/10 tests passing. No test asserts any number from results.txt, so headline results 2, 3 and 5 can regress silently.

The 'locate' variant is linear interpolation of a quadratic trajectory, a strawman for event location; the claim that it is the worst scheme (-30.8%) is disclosed as 'this crude implementation' but the study never includes the standard exact-quadratic-root event location, so the paper cannot say what a proper event-detecting twin does, which is the question its title poses.

README abstract item (5) states calibration 'does nothing at 1e-3 to 3e-3' without saying this is clamp only; for locate it improves at every step (-13.1 to -7.8%, -4.4 to -2.8%) and for mirror it flips sign. Mirror +53% at dt=1e-2 is a bisection landing on a discontinuity, an artefact of the calibration procedure rather than evidence about mirror twins.

Novelty is low: closed-form Zeno time and its e-derivative are textbook, and O(dt) bias of explicit time-stepping of Newton impact is the known order in the Moreau/Acary-Brogliato literature; no comparison with that literature, with a real engine (MuJoCo, PyBullet) or with data, so it does not reach the PhD-level programme bar in research/CLAUDE.md.
Mutation to zeno_time (x1.001) makes the test helper exact_height loop forever instead of failing: no loop guard, so a regression hangs CI.

No input validation: e >= 1 hangs last_time_above (infinite while loop) and divides by zero in zeno_time; delta >= h0 raises a math domain error; settle_twin silently truncates if the twin is still above delta at the hand-picked T = 1.4*exact + 1.
run.py section 6 re-implements the clamp loop inline instead of calling simulate (copied engine), so it would not follow a fix to simulate.

The first-order slope claim (1.0 to 1.1) is a five-point log-log fit of |error| that includes non-monotone cells; e_eff reads the apex off the step grid and is non-monotone in dt (clamp 0.89962 at 3e-3, 0.89984 at 1e-4), so its own error is comparable to the bias at fine steps.
defects.where: research/impact-twin/experiments/run.py section 2 and slope(); src/impact_twin/model.py e_eff

verdict: A small, honest, deterministic piece of work whose numbers are right: I rebuilt the Zeno time, its log-derivative (10.526, 100.50), the exact 1 cm settling time (7.6603 s), the clamp twin's -19.6% and -1.7% settling errors and its 0.8859 apparent restitution with a separate script, and the full experiment re-run is byte-identical to the committed results.txt. It is finished as scoped. It misses the bar on two fronts the rubric makes hard: verification (seeded bugs in the locate scheme and mirror factor passed all 10 tests, and no test asserts a reported twin number) and claims (result 4 compares a log change in Zeno time with a relative error of a different observable and calls it 'most' of the error; the README compresses result 5 so that it reads as general when it is clamp only). On research value it is a classroom-grade demonstration of a known O(dt) effect with a strawman 'locate' scheme and no comparison with a real engine, a published time-stepping analysis or data; a contact-dynamics reviewer would not find a publishable result. Meets the bar: no (verification 2, claims 2). Finished: yes.
